findings.claim: Elastane (brand name Lycra) is a polyurethane-based fibre capable of stretching to five to seven times its original length and recovering fully (some sources cite up to 8×; 5–6× is the most commonly cited figure) and recovering fully.
findings.truth: Elastane stretches to about five times its original length and recovers. The sentence also carries a drafting note that was never removed (the bracketed 'some sources cite...' aside) and repeats 'and recovering fully' twice, so the student is shown three different figures in one sentence.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Spandex: 'stretching up to five times its length'.

findings.claim: [1].q: 'Which synthetic fibre can stretch up to eight times its original length and recover fully?'
findings.truth: Elastane stretches to about five times its original length. 'Eight times' is wrong and contradicts the lesson text. The keyed answer (Elastane, index 2) stays correct, so only the question stem needs changing.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Spandex; consistency with corrected F1 text.

findings.claim: conventional cotton production uses roughly 6% of the world's pesticides despite occupying only 2.4% of its farmland (repeated in lesson 5, practice question 6 mark scheme)
findings.truth: The land share is sound (Wikipedia gives 2.5% of world arable land). The pesticide share is the older campaign figure; industry data from the late 2010s put cotton nearer 4.7% of pesticide sales and about 10% of insecticides, and no allowed source confirms 6%. Options: (a) leave it, since it is the figure most GCSE textbooks still print and no mark hangs on it; (b) replace the number with the comparison itself, e.g. 'uses far more pesticide than its 2.5% share of the world's cropland'. Recommendation: leave it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Cotton: '2.5% of the world's arable land'; no pesticide share given.
findings.ruling: NOTE: 6% pesticide share is the standard textbook figure; no permitted source contradicts it and no mark hangs on it - leave

findings.claim: a buttonhole foot for automatic four-step buttonholes
findings.truth: A four-step buttonhole is the semi-automatic method: the sewer turns a dial through four stages. The automatic version is the one-step buttonhole, where the foot holds the button and sets the length. The two are conflated here. It sits in a collapsible aside and costs no marks.

findings.claim: Legally required for children's nightwear (UK Night Clothes Safety Regulations), upholstered furniture and contract (public building) soft furnishings.
findings.truth: No such statute exists. The UK instrument is the Nightwear (Safety) Regulations 1985 (SI 1985/2043). The lesson's Key Fact box then tells students to 'always mention specific legislation' in the exam, so the invented name is what they would write.
findings.evidence: legislation.gov.uk, The Nightwear (Safety) Regulations 1985 (1985 No. 2043), regulation 4 'Requirements relating to children's nightwear'.

findings.claim: [7].a: 'UK Night Clothes Safety Regulations require it to reduce the risk of burn injuries if the fabric comes near a flame.'
findings.truth: Same invented statute name as F5, in the card a student would revise from. The correct name is the Nightwear (Safety) Regulations 1985.

findings.claim: This paired structure — one advantage, one limitation per method — is exactly what the mark scheme rewards at 6 and 8 marks.
findings.truth: This states as fact what a board's mark scheme rewards. The spec describes only 'a mix of short answer, structured and extended writing questions' for the 2-hour, 100-mark written paper and publishes no such rule. The advice itself is sound; the claim about the mark scheme is not.
findings.evidence: spec, Summary of Assessment (written examination: 2 hours, 50% of qualification, 100 marks).

findings.claim: responsible for approximately 10% of global carbon emissions and 20% of industrial water pollution
findings.truth: The 10% figure comes from a 2018 press release and is not supported by the studies since. Fashion is now put at roughly 2% to 8% of global greenhouse-gas emissions (a 2021 WRI study gives about 2%; the UN Economic Commission for Europe quotes 2-8%). The 20% water-pollution figure is sound and stays.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Environmental impact of fashion: 'In the late 2010s fashion emitted 2-4% of world total greenhouse gases'; the 8% figure described as outdated; 'roughly one-fifth of all industrial water pollution'.

findings.claim: Post-consumer textile recycling rates remain below 1% globally despite growing collection infrastructure.
findings.truth: The under-1% figure is for fibre-to-fibre recycling only, that is clothing recycled back into new clothing. Far more than 1% of used textiles is collected and downcycled into insulation, wiping cloths and felt, which the lesson has just described. As written the sentence contradicts its own paragraph.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Environmental impact of fashion: 'Less than one percent of clothing is recycled to make new clothes.'

findings.claim: A single wash of a polyester fleece jacket can shed over 700,000 fibres. (Lesson 1 carries the same figure for 'a fleece jacket'.)
findings.truth: The 700,000 figure is per wash load, not per jacket, and the fabric that shed that many in the study was acrylic; polyester shed fewer. The examinable point, that synthetics shed microfibres in the wash, stands, so no edit.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Microfiber, citing 'Single clothes wash may release 700,000 microplastic fibres'.

findings.truth: Mass production and continuous production are separate scales in the wider D&T vocabulary: continuous runs non-stop, day and night, on one product. The bullet itself describes mass production correctly, and the spec names only job, batch and mass production, so no edit. The spec's own term for the organisation of the line is 'line production'.
findings.evidence: spec, in-depth textiles section 5: 'job production (custom-made or one-off); batch production; mass production' and 'line production; progressive bundle system; cell production'.

summary: Eleven findings across four lessons: two invented-legislation instances (the 'UK Night Clothes Safety Regulations', which does not exist, in both the lesson text and a flashcard), an unfinished drafting note left inside the elastane sentence with a knowledge check keyed to a third figure, an invented mark-scheme claim, and two out-of-date sustainability statistics. Fibre sources, weave and knit structures, seam types, dye and print process-fabric pairings and every knowledge-check answer key are correct throughout; no lesson names the board.
